label: rem:fourier-mukai-and-orlov
title: Fourier–Mukai transforms and Orlov's theorem: where a derived realisation would close a gap
html:
The equivalences this paper uses are Tannakian — a quantum observable universe is reconstructed from its fibre functor as \mathbf{C} \simeq \mathrm{Rep}(H) — and Tannakian equivalences are monoidal, not derived. This remark records what the derived language would add, where it could close a gap, and why it does not do so at present.

The transform. For smooth projective varieties X and Y and an object K of the bounded derived category D^{b}(X \times Y), the Fourier–Mukai transform with kernel K is the functor \Phi_{K} \colon D^{b}(X) \to D^{b}(Y), E \mapsto Rp_{Y*}(p_{X}^{*}E \otimes^{L} K): pull back, tensor with the kernel, push forward. Orlov's theorem states that every fully faithful exact functor D^{b}(X) \to D^{b}(Y) is of this form, with K unique up to isomorphism [orlov1997]. On the base curve itself the transform buys nothing: by Bondal and Orlov a smooth projective curve of genus at least two is determined by its derived category, and its autoequivalences are generated by automorphisms, twists by line bundles and shifts, \mathrm{Aut}(D^{b}(M_{0})) = \mathrm{Aut}(M_{0}) \ltimes \mathrm{Pic}(M_{0}) \times \mathbb{Z} [bondal-orlov2001]. There is no hidden derived partner of Bring's curve.

Where it would help. What the paper does not have is a trace map from the substrate to the base — a map under which the Chern character of a substrate object becomes a class on M_{0}, so that the Hochschild homology of the substrate and the Hochschild homology of the curve, which the Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg theorem identifies with \bigoplus_{i} H^{i}(M_{0}, \Omega^{i+n}), are compared by a canonical map rather than by an assumed one. An integral transform supplies exactly this. A functor \Phi_{K} \colon \mathcal{D}(A) \to D^{b}(M_{0}) induces a map HH_{\bullet}(\Phi_{K}) on Hochschild homology, canonically, and that map is the correspondence defined by the Chern character of the kernel, \mathrm{ch}(K) \in HH_{0}(X \times Y), by the theorem of Căldăraru and Willerton [caldararu-willerton-2010]. That is a construction, and it forces numbers: the Hochschild homology of the curve has dimensions 2, 4, 4 in degrees 0, \pm 1 and its Hochschild cohomology 1, 4, 9 in degrees 0, 1, 2, with S_{5}-invariant parts 2, 0, 0 and 1, 0, 0 (the three Euler characteristics); a substrate mapped to the curve by a fully faithful transform would have to carry the same, and the Euler characteristic of Bring's surface would be the alternating sum of a map, not of a coincidence.

Why it does not apply yet. Orlov's theorem needs a functor between bounded derived categories of smooth projective varieties. The paper's archimedean realisation is the spatial realisation functor, which lands in modules over the ground ring — the fibre functor takes values in R-\mathbf{Mod}, not in a derived category of the base — and no object of the substrate is given as a complex of sheaves on M_{0}. Stating the realisation at the derived level, with a kernel on \mathrm{Spec}(A) \times M_{0}, is the missing step; it is a definition to be made, not a theorem to be proved, and until it is made the comparison of Hochschild theories in this chapter is a comparison of dimensions, not of maps.
